extracted.intended_audience: readers of Jefferson correspondence; historians and students of constitutional and early American political thought
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of Thomas Jefferson's 1788 letters giving normative recommendations on constitutional design, a bill of rights, civil liberties (jury, habeas corpus, press, religion), standing armies and militia, monopolies, rotation in office, and related policy/administrative practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extreme constitutional 'bracing'
rubrics_metrics.description: "We must take care not to run from one extreme to another; not to brace too high."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates moderate reform rather than over-correcting; warns against adopting extremes in designing government institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill of Rights — necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: "I join those in opinion, who think a bill of rights necessary."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates core protections expected in such a bill (trial by jury, habeas corpus, limits on standing armies, freedom of the press, freedom of religion, suppression of monopolies). If general exceptions cannot be agreed, better to establish these rights universally than not at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trials by jury
rubrics_metrics.description: "It seems pretty generally understood, that this should go to juries... I conceive there may be difficulty in finding general modifications of these, suited to the habits of all the States. But if such cannot be found, then it is better to establish trials by jury... in all cases."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an exception (e.g., disputes between a foreigner and a native) cannot be agreed, model the jury by providing the medietas linguæ (half-language/right of use) in civil as well as criminal cases as a compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of the right of habeas corpus
rubrics_metrics.description: "Why suspend the habeas corpus in insurrections and rebellions? The parties who may be arrested, may be charged instantly with a well-defined crime..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against routine suspension; if temporary detention is needed, the accused should be tried, remanded and retried while necessity continues, and be given redress (damages) against the government. Cites English history to show suspensions often unjustified and become habitual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the press with liability for false facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration, that the federal government will never restrain the presses from printing any thing they please, will not take away the liability of the printers for false facts printed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports a categorical non-restriction on printing by government while preserving civil/criminal accountability (libel, damages) for false statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of religion does not excuse criminal acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration, that religious faith shall be unpunished, does not give impunity to criminal acts, dictated by religious error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious protections should not be interpreted as blanket immunity from prosecution for criminal behavior motivated by religious belief or error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish standing armies in time of peace; favor militia
rubrics_metrics.description: "Abolish standing armies in time of peace... If no check can be found to keep the number of standing troops within safe bounds, while they are tolerated as far as necessary, abandon them altogether, discipline well the militia, and guard the magazines with them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where standing armies are politically risky, rely on well-disciplined militia and minimal magazine guards; warns that more than magazine guards is 'useless' if few and 'dangerous' if many; asserts that no European nation can realistically send a regular army to threaten the U.S., and militia should suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose monopolies generally
rubrics_metrics.description: "There shall be no monopolies... The saying--there shall be no monopolies, lessens the incitements to ingenuity, which is spurred on by the hope of a monopoly for a limited time, as of fourteen years; but the benefit of even limited monopolies is too doubtful, to be opposed to that of their general suppression."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that limited monopolies (e.g., 14-year terms) may encourage innovation, but contends their public benefit is too doubtful to justify keeping monopolies; favors their general suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation in office (term limits) to prevent abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: "I apprehend too, that the total abandonment of the principle of rotation in the offices of President and Senator, will end in abuse."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates maintaining rotation/periodic turnover in office-holding to prevent concentration of power and corruption; notes public opinion varies by office (e.g., President vs. Senate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer peaceful institutional change; avoid appeal to arms
rubrics_metrics.description: "If they can avoid the appeal to arms, the nation will be sure to gain much by this controversy. But if that appeal is made, it will depend entirely on the disposition of the army, whether it issue in liberty or despotism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages civic and constitutional remedies over armed conflict; warns that resort to arms hands decisive power to the army and risks despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: When exceptions cannot be agreed, favor universal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: "If proper exceptions to these general rules are desirable, and probably practicable, yet if the exceptions cannot be agreed on, the establishment of the rules, in all cases, will do ill in very few."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy principle: prefer clear, broadly-applied rights rather than complex, narrowly-carved exceptions that may undermine protection in the majority of cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat potentially sensitive documents cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding a man who offered Silas Deane's account books and letters: Jefferson examined them and thought 'it desirable that they should not come to the hands of the British minister' but did not purchase them without authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering documents that could be damaging if handed to adversaries, assess their value and consider purchasing or securing them only with proper authority; avoid unauthorized dissemination to foreign powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain domestic debt to preserve financial credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "The transfer of these debts to Europe will excessively embarrass, and perhaps totally prevent the borrowing any money in Europe, till these shall be paid off. This is a momentous object, and, in my opinion, should receive instantaneous attention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for keeping the national/public debt within the country to avoid undermining ability to borrow abroad and to protect the nation's financial position; references his letter to the treasury with suggested means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark recommendation letters by source of endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: "I will beg the favor of you to distinguish the letters wherein I appeal to recommendations from other persons, from those which I write on my own knowledge."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural guidance for recommendations: explicitly label whether a recommendation is based on the writer's personal knowledge or is a third-party appeal, to avoid compromising endorsers or misleading recipients.
